newsitem.title: HONG KONG: Future uncertain for HK libel laws, expert says.
newsitem.headline: Future uncertain for HK libel laws, expert says.

text.p: Hong Kong has done better than most of Asia in avoiding abuse of libel laws to crimp people's freedoms but there are fears things could get worse after the handover to China in 1997, a legal expert said on Wednesday.
"I think Hong Kong is infinitely better (than the rest of Asia)," Geoffrey Miles, a lawyer with 25 years of experience in Hong Kong, told Reuters after a seminar.
"The number of defamation actions which have been brought in Hong Kong is very small, " he told a Foreign Correspondents' Club seminar on the use of libel laws to curb press freedom.
"I have not seen any series of writs issued by any one individual over a long period of time."
An independent judiciary was a "strong safeguard" against the abuse of defamation laws in the territory, Miles, one of the territory's leading experts on libel, said.
"I think Hong Kong is very good (in safeguarding against abuse of defamation laws)," he said. "But whether it will remain so, it is very much a matter of speculation."
Britain hands the colony back to China at midnight next June 30. Beijing keeps a tight rein on the media and Hong Kong journalists are jittery over press freedom after the sovereignty transfer.
In the seminar, Hong Kong-based journalists, already upset about libel laws being used to gag the press, expressed their concerns over abuse after 1997.
Newspapers "are concerned that the libel laws will be utilised in such a way as to stifle their freedom to report on sensitive issues", Miles said.

Howie Severino, a reporter based in the Philippines, said libel laws could be used to "silence or punish journalists who are trying to perform their duties" and "to mute reporting of misconduct and criticism of public policy".
The time-consuming procedures in fighting litigation alone could deter newspapers from reporting sensitive facts, he said.
While China has promised Hong Kong's capitalist system will remains largely unchanged for 50 years after 1997, "only time will tell whether that is correct or not", Miles said.
A string of developments this year escalated fears over a clampdown on press freedoms after the handover.
Beijing has objected to London's proposal to introduce in the colony a liberal anti-subversion bill that sets legal markers against China-style jailings of dissidents.

Lu Ping, the senior Chinese official in charge of Hong Kong affairs, has warned that Hong Kong media will not be allowed to advocate anti-constitutional ideas and Foreign Minister Qian Qichen has said press freedom will be limited after 1997.
